Stem-Cell Therapy for Autism - A Medical Conundrum

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell therapy for autism. How effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?

Unique Selling Point:
Stem-cell therapy is growing in prominence in the medical world, reporting to effectively treat an increasing number of devastating and debilitating diseases, including autism. Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell treatment, but how effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?

Summary:
Stem Cell therapy is a buzzword in the medical fraternity with practitioners hailing it as a medical breakthrough. In oncology in particular, stem cells have been used for decades to treat certain cancers such as leukemia through bone marrow transplants. Dr Alok Sharma from the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai, India claims and believes that stem-cell therapy is a revolution for treating autistic people. The endorsement of stem-cell therapy has taken hold in the East and South America, especially in China, India and Panama. However, various applications of the treatment have been met with skepticism in the mainstream medical fraternity. Experts, such as Dr Lawrence Goldstein, Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center, suggest that stem-cell therapy for autism is a bogus treatment that has not been clinically proven and can be a fruitless and expensive exercise for desperate people. On the other hand, a number of parents who have put their children through this procedure vow that they can see and experience great improvements in their children. As well as interviewing medical experts, Carte Blanche gets to talk to some of these parents and care givers who swear by the treatment and say it could be the miracle they have been waiting for. Carte Blanche investigates, is this treatment bogus or is there real hope for the autistic?

Further information:
Autism is a genetic disorder that indicates abnormalities in numerous areas of the brain. The traits of autistic people usually involve: lack of verbal and non-verbal communication, lack of social interaction along with restricted and repetitive behaviour. They are locked in a world of their own and find it very hard to intuitively react to the things we so often take for granted. For people with autism the world as we know it is mostly a foreign place. Continuous hand flapping, head rolling and self-injury are some of the early symptoms that signal autism in children.
There are educational and behavioural therapies that form part of treatment for autism but there is yet to be a proven medical procedure that totally eradicates or reverses the illness. This has created frustrations and desperation for autistic people and their families. They are often driven to searching for alternative treatments. Other treatments, such as dietary supplements and art related therapies, are the routes parents have taken to help their children. Even though parents and care givers often vouch that they can see visible improvements, these treatments have not been proven conclusively and often appear to be a waste of money. They can be easy prey for scamsters and charlatans.
Dr Alok Sharma from the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai, India believes that stem-cell therapy is a medical breakthrough for autistic people. Neuro Regenerative Rehabilitation Therapy, as Dr Sharma calls it, is a medical procedure where stem-cells are taken from the patient’s hipbone and injected into the spine. According to Dr Sharma this is a safe and risk free procedure that has proven to show vast improvements in his patients. Parents that have taken their children for this procedure rave about the results. They attest to improvements in the behavioural condition of the kids. However, these claims have been met with negative responses by some of the experts in the stem-cell and neurological field, as there has not been a conclusive clinical study that proves that stem cells can improve Autism or many other of the neurological diseases it purports to treat.
According to Dr Lawrence Goldstein Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center in the USA, stem-cell treatment for autism can be misleading to desperate people and prove to be a terribly expensive exercise. Furthermore, the treatment can be a serious risk for the patients as it may cause tumors and growths in the brains of the patient. However, Dr Alok Sharma believes it is a safe procedure and he can help a lot of people in need. He also claims that it is only embryonic stem cell transplants that cause growths and that it is safe to remove stem cells from the hip bone.
This is a treatment that has not been approved in the South African medical field due to the lack of clinical evidence. This has not dissuaded parents, those with sufficient funds, who have travelled as far as India in search of a glimmer of hope for their children.
Mimmie Ralph is a parent with an Autistic Child. She shares her experience with us, of her son De Wet, from the day he was born to the day he was diagnosed with Autism. Mimmie also tells us about how the journey of living with an autistic child has been and how it has impacted her life. Along her journey she has also tried numerous ways to get help for her son.
Victor is a young boy from Kenya who also suffers from Autism. His mother Jacinta Waruru, tells us of Victor’s early years with Autism. Jacinta also shares the journey that they have gone through in trying to find help for their son. What adjustments they have made in their lives to accommodate him and his disability.
Dr Sharma tells us about his procedure and how it really works. He claims the bone marrow that makes blood has scores of stem cells. These cells are removed from the bone marrow and put in the patient’s lower back through injection. These cells travel all the way to the brain and help the recovery of the patient.
He also shares with us the proven cases with PET scans that show the improvement of his patients. He gives us his perspective as to the reasons behind why. There is a widespread disagreement, in the medical fraternity, against the ability for Stem cell therapy to improve Autism with many doctors and neurologists suggesting that there is no conclusive proof that stem cell treatment does work on autistic patients and, in fact, that this may be very dangerous for the patients.
Dr Lawrence Goldstein Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center tells us over Skype why he has reservations with this application of stem-cell treatment. Dr Goldstein also shares with us his vast understanding when it comes to stem cells in general and why he thinks this procedure might be risky. According to Dr Goldstein children with Autism generally show progress and that unless there is a proper clinical trial with Stem Cell therapy for Autism, it can never be clear that this treatment actually works.
Andelene Thysse, who has an autistic son, runs a De Grendel home and learning centre for Autistic children. She believes that this procedure works and that it is the shining light that Autism patients, and their parents alike, have been waiting for. According to Andelene some of the kids she takes care of have shown immense progress in a very short space of time since they received the treatment from Dr Alok Sharma. She shares with us the improvements she has seen in the kids since they were treated.
A top South African Neurologist, Dr David Griessel takes a look at some of the PET scans from Dr Alok’s patients that have shown the supposed improvement. The Neurologist will also impart his knowledge of stem cells and whether he believes the treatment can cure Autism. Furthermore, Dr Griessel will give his considered medical opinion on whether this is a viable option for autistic people.
Jacinta Waruru and Mimie Ralph share with us the improvements they have observed in their Autistic children. They describe to us how their kids have been behaving differently and whether they believe in this procedure or not. Is this a procedure they would recommend to other parents? The parents also discuss the financial implications that are involved with having this procedure done. Is it an affordable route for all parents?
The issue remains that Autism is a frustrating condition for parents who have Autistic kids, but when there is no ray of light for them can they really sit back and fold their arms? With Dr Sharma’s treatment clearly being supported by some parents, is this the medical discovery that the world has been waiting for or is it just another medical scam for the desperate?

Press Release:


Stem-cell therapy is growing in prominence in the medical world, reporting to effectively treat an increasing number of devastating and debilitating diseases, including autism. Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell treatment, but how effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?

Script:


Miemie: Can you imagine living in a world – where you can't speak to somebody – you can't tell somebody your needs, or tell somebody that your'e thirsty or hungry – if he try and want to communicate with me, he can't do that, he will actually start biting his hand or hitting his head – the hardest part about living with a kid with Autism is the feeling of helplessness. (Kiss)

Link: Autism spectrum disorder is a debilitating neurological illness with no known cure. For the severely autistic it is a life sentence of dependance and isolation. Over the years there have been many treatments that have promised to alleviate the condition with little or no results.

VO: De Wet is 6 years old, he was diagnosed at the age of 3 as severely autistic. Over the years he has undergone various therapies but his mother Miemie Ralph found his progress slow.(unresponsive)

Miemie: We've done several kinds of therapy.
Just endlessly searching for an answer to improve his quality of life.

(Sound up)
Miemie: De Wet wat wil jy doen?

VO: Dr Griessel a neurologist and developmental paediatrician at Universitas Hospital in Bloemfontein has been treating autistic patients since 1990

Dr Griessel: We know a lot more about autism than we did a few years back but there are many unanswered questions because every child is unique.

You will have to differentiate between treatments that have stood the test of time the ones that have been evaluated and found useful are basically therapies like speech therapy, Occupational therapy and then also something called developmental interventions, which try work through the autism.

VO: Andelene Thysse spent many years searching for answers for her Autistic son Frikkie, who is now 32.

Andelene: There was nobody to guard you theres no professionals, you just been told that your child is now autistic and you have to cope with it.

VO: She responded by founding the De Grendel home and Learning Centre for autistic children and adults, in Cape Town.

Andelene: Currently I've got 6 boys but they vary from the ages of 7 to 32 where my son is the oldest.

VO: When one of the parent's of the children in Andelene's care, suggested there was possible new stem cell treatment for autism in Mumbai India that could help their son, she was very skeptical at first - but one trip to India changed her mind.

Link: Stem-cell therapy is the new miracle buzz word amongst the medical fraternity, opening up possibilities of treating a number of neurological diseases, like ALS, cerebral palsy, and now autism, but is there enough medical proof that it really does work?

VO: Dr Sharma of the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai India, believes there is.

Dr Sharma: This is objective proof that the damage in the brain has been resolved.

VO: Dr Sharma is presenting his procedure in Randfontein. This treatment is not available in South Africa and desperate people are hoping for a miracle cure all.

Dr Sharma: I have been doing stem cell therapy for the last 8 years and I have treated so far, a little over 5000 patients of different diseases. I'd slowly realised that children tended to respond much better to stem cell therapy and so subsequently autism also started getting treated.

VO: Dr Sharma claims he has documented a 91% success rate of improvement with autism. The best results have been with younger children.

Dr Sharma: One of the first things that happens after we give them some therapies, is that their hyper activity disappears and the children become completely cooperative, now they are more responsive to therapy. We have children who can get back into the normal education system.

VO: There are a number of ways that stem cells can be harvested. This procedure involves removing the stem cells from the bone marrow in the hip bone of the patient, and re-injecting it back through the spine.

Dr Sharma: Now the cerebral spine fluid will carry this directly to the brain, once it reaches the brain what happens is the parts that are damaged, attract the stem cells towards them and then the process of repair then starts.

VO: Dr Sharma has tracked the PET scans of over 600 patients.

Dr Sharma: When we do a PET scan it actually looks at which part of the brain is working normally, which is working more and which is working less. So you can actually see the functional damage on a pet scan and we have seen this resolve after stem cell therapy.

VO: Dr Griessel on the other hand, is not convinced that the PET scans actually show visible repair.

Dr Griessel: Scans just often tell us that this part lights up so its a little more active than it was before. it doesn't actually tell us, that this child is functioning better.

VO: When Miemie Ralph heard about this stem-cell procedure, she knew she had to give it a try. De Wet had his first stem-cell transplant in January this year in India and she says the results were visible after the first month of his treatment.

Miemie: De Wet didn't have any ball sense, he couldn’t throw a ball Now he can understand like pick up the ball, bring the ball, throw the ball.

We actually got him to be able to sit down, and he started to feed himself. Something that he couldn't do.

Dr Griessel: Very rarely people and parents would just do one thing, they would continue with therapy, many children with autism get significantly smarter over time. So that makes it really difficult to say that because I've done this stem cell therapy then the improvement must be due to the stem cell.

VO: One of the key elements to Dr Sharma's stem-cell treatment is the intensified post transplant additional therapies that need to be adhered to. Since Andelene's first trip to India she has supervised a few autistic children through stem-cell treatment.

Andelene: We do post therapy in south africa which is an amazing achievement to see their progress.

VO: One such child is 14 year old Victor Wareru from Kenya, who has already undergone 3 transplants since the age of 12.
Jacinta, Victor's mother, says the improvement in him has been visible and dramatic

Jacinta: From since he was born to the age of 12 he was still very hyper there was no improvement at all, but the first stem cell was when we had started noticing some changes, in the hyper activity, in the concentration, in the aggressiveness.

VO: After his 3rd Stem cell transplant, Victor can now ride a bicycle, play baseball and even swim.

Dr Griessel: Stem cell therapy for neurological disorders are really a very exciting field, but whether we are already there, to recommend it as a standard treatment, I'm not so sure.

Dr Sharma: We have the facts, we have patient documentation and we have published literature.

Link: Stem cell therapy is used to treat autism in countries such as China, India and some parts of South America, but experts warn of bogus treatments that are yet to be clinically proven.

VO: We connected via skype with Dr Lawrence Goldstein one of the world's leading experts in stem-cell research at Sanford Clinical Centre in the US. They are currently in the process of conducting their own clinical trials.

Dr Lawrence Goldstein: Stem cell therapy is very promising and has a great deal of experimental work that needs to be done, to find out how best to use stem cells for treatment.

That said, we have a world wide problem with clinics springing up all over the world selling unproven therapies to hopeful parents.

VO: And the kind of stem cell therapy offered at the Neurogen Clinic in India, comes at a price - $11 000 dollars per treatment.

Dr Lawrence Goldstein: It is unethical to be charging parents $11 000 dollars to treat a child with the therapy that may or may not actually work.

Dr Griessel: The money that someone uses for that is money that's not available in the long term for their children for therapy, or for a trust fund, so I would like better evidence.

Dr Lawrence Goldstein: Having read Dr Sharma's papers they just don't make a lot of sense scientifically, and thats why the burden of proof is on the investigator who's charging people money, to demonstrate properly that the therapy works

Dr Sharma: The answer to the ethical basis of this, is something called the Helsinki Declaration of the World Medical Association it says, for a patient suffering from a condition for which there is no treatment, or all treatment options have been exhausted, a physician has a right to use an unproven therapy, if in the physician's judgement it can save life or improve the quality of the patient.

Dr Griessel: I think it cannot be recommended at this stage in time. I think parents should wait for the results of randomized control trials.

VO: But conclusive evidence could be some 3 to 10 years away. So where does that leave those who are needing help now?

Miemie: There is no cure for Autism. I would almost try anything with him, whatever can improve your child's life you will take that.

FIN

PROMO 1: 15”

VO: Without any known cure, could cutting edge stem-cell therapy provide the answer to treating Autism Spectrum disorder? One doctor believes it does.

Dr Sharma: Their hyper activity dissappears.



PROMO 2. 15”

VO: Stem-cell therapy is the new medical buzz word, treating a number of diseases including Autism. Mainstream medical circles are skeptical.

Dr Griessel: Whether we are already there to recommend it as a standard treatment, I'm not so sure.


PROMO 10”

VO: Many people with Autism spectrum disorder carry the burden of living with an incurable condition. Could stem cell therapy be the hope that changes their lives //( for the better?)

Last Updated 04 June 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 06 June 2017 Press Release: Stem-cell therapy is growing in prominence in the medical world, reporting to effectively treat an increasing number of devastating and debilitating diseases, including autism. Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell treatment, but how effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them? Script: Miemie: Can you imagine living in a world – where you can't speak to somebody – you can't tell somebody your needs, or tell somebody that your'e thirsty or hungry – if he try and want to communicate with me, he can't do that, he will actually start biting his hand or hitting his head – the hardest part about living with a kid with Autism is the feeling of helplessness. (Kiss) Link: Autism spectrum disorder is a debilitating neurological illness with no known cure. For the severely autistic it is a life sentence of dependance and isolation. Over the years there have been many treatments that have promised to alleviate the condition with little or no results. VO: De Wet is 6 years old, he was diagnosed at the age of 3 as severely autistic. Over the years he has undergone various therapies but his mother Miemie Ralph found his progress slow.(unresponsive) Miemie: We've done several kinds of therapy. Just endlessly searching for an answer to improve his quality of life. (Sound up) Miemie: De Wet wat wil jy doen? VO: Dr Griessel a neurologist and developmental paediatrician at Universitas Hospital in Bloemfontein has been treating autistic patients since 1990 Dr Griessel: We know a lot more about autism than we did a few years back but there are many unanswered questions because every child is unique. You will have to differentiate between treatments that have stood the test of time the ones that have been evaluated and found useful are basically therapies like speech therapy, Occupational therapy and then also something called developmental interventions, which try work through the autism. VO: Andelene Thysse spent many years searching for answers for her Autistic son Frikkie, who is now 32. Andelene: There was nobody to guard you theres no professionals, you just been told that your child is now autistic and you have to cope with it. VO: She responded by founding the De Grendel home and Learning Centre for autistic children and adults, in Cape Town. Andelene: Currently I've got 6 boys but they vary from the ages of 7 to 32 where my son is the oldest. VO: When one of the parent's of the children in Andelene's care, suggested there was possible new stem cell treatment for autism in Mumbai India that could help their son, she was very skeptical at first - but one trip to India changed her mind. Link: Stem-cell therapy is the new miracle buzz word amongst the medical fraternity, opening up possibilities of treating a number of neurological diseases, like ALS, cerebral palsy, and now autism, but is there enough medical proof that it really does work? VO: Dr Sharma of the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai India, believes there is. Dr Sharma: This is objective proof that the damage in the brain has been resolved. VO: Dr Sharma is presenting his procedure in Randfontein. This treatment is not available in South Africa and desperate people are hoping for a miracle cure all. Dr Sharma: I have been doing stem cell therapy for the last 8 years and I have treated so far, a little over 5000 patients of different diseases. I'd slowly realised that children tended to respond much better to stem cell therapy and so subsequently autism also started getting treated. VO: Dr Sharma claims he has documented a 91% success rate of improvement with autism. The best results have been with younger children. Dr Sharma: One of the first things that happens after we give them some therapies, is that their hyper activity disappears and the children become completely cooperative, now they are more responsive to therapy. We have children who can get back into the normal education system. VO: There are a number of ways that stem cells can be harvested. This procedure involves removing the stem cells from the bone marrow in the hip bone of the patient, and re-injecting it back through the spine. Dr Sharma: Now the cerebral spine fluid will carry this directly to the brain, once it reaches the brain what happens is the parts that are damaged, attract the stem cells towards them and then the process of repair then starts. VO: Dr Sharma has tracked the PET scans of over 600 patients. Dr Sharma: When we do a PET scan it actually looks at which part of the brain is working normally, which is working more and which is working less. So you can actually see the functional damage on a pet scan and we have seen this resolve after stem cell therapy. VO: Dr Griessel on the other hand, is not convinced that the PET scans actually show visible repair. Dr Griessel: Scans just often tell us that this part lights up so its a little more active than it was before. it doesn't actually tell us, that this child is functioning better. VO: When Miemie Ralph heard about this stem-cell procedure, she knew she had to give it a try. De Wet had his first stem-cell transplant in January this year in India and she says the results were visible after the first month of his treatment. Miemie: De Wet didn't have any ball sense, he couldn’t throw a ball Now he can understand like pick up the ball, bring the ball, throw the ball. We actually got him to be able to sit down, and he started to feed himself. Something that he couldn't do. Dr Griessel: Very rarely people and parents would just do one thing, they would continue with therapy, many children with autism get significantly smarter over time. So that makes it really difficult to say that because I've done this stem cell therapy then the improvement must be due to the stem cell. VO: One of the key elements to Dr Sharma's stem-cell treatment is the intensified post transplant additional therapies that need to be adhered to. Since Andelene's first trip to India she has supervised a few autistic children through stem-cell treatment. Andelene: We do post therapy in south africa which is an amazing achievement to see their progress. VO: One such child is 14 year old Victor Wareru from Kenya, who has already undergone 3 transplants since the age of 12. Jacinta, Victor's mother, says the improvement in him has been visible and dramatic Jacinta: From since he was born to the age of 12 he was still very hyper there was no improvement at all, but the first stem cell was when we had started noticing some changes, in the hyper activity, in the concentration, in the aggressiveness. VO: After his 3rd Stem cell transplant, Victor can now ride a bicycle, play baseball and even swim. Dr Griessel: Stem cell therapy for neurological disorders are really a very exciting field, but whether we are already there, to recommend it as a standard treatment, I'm not so sure. Dr Sharma: We have the facts, we have patient documentation and we have published literature. Link: Stem cell therapy is used to treat autism in countries such as China, India and some parts of South America, but experts warn of bogus treatments that are yet to be clinically proven. VO: We connected via skype with Dr Lawrence Goldstein one of the world's leading experts in stem-cell research at Sanford Clinical Centre in the US. They are currently in the process of conducting their own clinical trials. Dr Lawrence Goldstein: Stem cell therapy is very promising and has a great deal of experimental work that needs to be done, to find out how best to use stem cells for treatment. That said, we have a world wide problem with clinics springing up all over the world selling unproven therapies to hopeful parents. VO: And the kind of stem cell therapy offered at the Neurogen Clinic in India, comes at a price - $11 000 dollars per treatment. Dr Lawrence Goldstein: It is unethical to be charging parents $11 000 dollars to treat a child with the therapy that may or may not actually work. Dr Griessel: The money that someone uses for that is money that's not available in the long term for their children for therapy, or for a trust fund, so I would like better evidence. Dr Lawrence Goldstein: Having read Dr Sharma's papers they just don't make a lot of sense scientifically, and thats why the burden of proof is on the investigator who's charging people money, to demonstrate properly that the therapy works Dr Sharma: The answer to the ethical basis of this, is something called the Helsinki Declaration of the World Medical Association it says, for a patient suffering from a condition for which there is no treatment, or all treatment options have been exhausted, a physician has a right to use an unproven therapy, if in the physician's judgement it can save life or improve the quality of the patient. Dr Griessel: I think it cannot be recommended at this stage in time. I think parents should wait for the results of randomized control trials. VO: But conclusive evidence could be some 3 to 10 years away. So where does that leave those who are needing help now? Miemie: There is no cure for Autism. I would almost try anything with him, whatever can improve your child's life you will take that. FIN PROMO 1: 15” VO: Without any known cure, could cutting edge stem-cell therapy provide the answer to treating Autism Spectrum disorder? One doctor believes it does. Dr Sharma: Their hyper activity dissappears. PROMO 2. 15” VO: Stem-cell therapy is the new medical buzz word, treating a number of diseases including Autism. Mainstream medical circles are skeptical. Dr Griessel: Whether we are already there to recommend it as a standard treatment, I'm not so sure. PROMO 10” VO: Many people with Autism spectrum disorder carry the burden of living with an incurable condition. Could stem cell therapy be the hope that changes their lives //( for the better?)

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Stem-cell therapy is growing in prominence in the medical world, reporting to effectively treat an increasing number of devastating and debilitating diseases, including autism. Desperate parents are sending their children to places like India for stem-cell treatment, but how effective are these therapies and what does the mainstream medical fraternity say about them?
metadata.Summary: Stem Cell therapy is a buzzword in the medical fraternity with practitioners hailing it as a medical breakthrough. In oncology in particular, stem cells have been used for decades to treat certain cancers such as leukemia through bone marrow transplants. Dr Alok Sharma from the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai, India claims and believes that stem-cell therapy is a revolution for treating autistic people. The endorsement of stem-cell therapy has taken hold in the East and South America, especially in China, India and Panama. However, various applications of the treatment have been met with skepticism in the mainstream medical fraternity. Experts, such as Dr Lawrence Goldstein, Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center, suggest that stem-cell therapy for autism is a bogus treatment that has not been clinically proven and can be a fruitless and expensive exercise for desperate people. On the other hand, a number of parents who have put their children through this procedure vow that they can see and experience great improvements in their children. As well as interviewing medical experts, Carte Blanche gets to talk to some of these parents and care givers who swear by the treatment and say it could be the miracle they have been waiting for. Carte Blanche investigates, is this treatment bogus or is there real hope for the autistic?
metadata.Further information: Autism is a genetic disorder that indicates abnormalities in numerous areas of the brain. The traits of autistic people usually involve: lack of verbal and non-verbal communication, lack of social interaction along with restricted and repetitive behaviour. They are locked in a world of their own and find it very hard to intuitively react to the things we so often take for granted. For people with autism the world as we know it is mostly a foreign place. Continuous hand flapping, head rolling and self-injury are some of the early symptoms that signal autism in children. There are educational and behavioural therapies that form part of treatment for autism but there is yet to be a proven medical procedure that totally eradicates or reverses the illness. This has created frustrations and desperation for autistic people and their families. They are often driven to searching for alternative treatments. Other treatments, such as dietary supplements and art related therapies, are the routes parents have taken to help their children. Even though parents and care givers often vouch that they can see visible improvements, these treatments have not been proven conclusively and often appear to be a waste of money. They can be easy prey for scamsters and charlatans. Dr Alok Sharma from the Neurogen Brain and Spine Institute in Mumbai, India believes that stem-cell therapy is a medical breakthrough for autistic people. Neuro Regenerative Rehabilitation Therapy, as Dr Sharma calls it, is a medical procedure where stem-cells are taken from the patient’s hipbone and injected into the spine. According to Dr Sharma this is a safe and risk free procedure that has proven to show vast improvements in his patients. Parents that have taken their children for this procedure rave about the results. They attest to improvements in the behavioural condition of the kids. However, these claims have been met with negative responses by some of the experts in the stem-cell and neurological field, as there has not been a conclusive clinical study that proves that stem cells can improve Autism or many other of the neurological diseases it purports to treat. According to Dr Lawrence Goldstein Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center in the USA, stem-cell treatment for autism can be misleading to desperate people and prove to be a terribly expensive exercise. Furthermore, the treatment can be a serious risk for the patients as it may cause tumors and growths in the brains of the patient. However, Dr Alok Sharma believes it is a safe procedure and he can help a lot of people in need. He also claims that it is only embryonic stem cell transplants that cause growths and that it is safe to remove stem cells from the hip bone. This is a treatment that has not been approved in the South African medical field due to the lack of clinical evidence. This has not dissuaded parents, those with sufficient funds, who have travelled as far as India in search of a glimmer of hope for their children. Mimmie Ralph is a parent with an Autistic Child. She shares her experience with us, of her son De Wet, from the day he was born to the day he was diagnosed with Autism. Mimmie also tells us about how the journey of living with an autistic child has been and how it has impacted her life. Along her journey she has also tried numerous ways to get help for her son. Victor is a young boy from Kenya who also suffers from Autism. His mother Jacinta Waruru, tells us of Victor’s early years with Autism. Jacinta also shares the journey that they have gone through in trying to find help for their son. What adjustments they have made in their lives to accommodate him and his disability. Dr Sharma tells us about his procedure and how it really works. He claims the bone marrow that makes blood has scores of stem cells. These cells are removed from the bone marrow and put in the patient’s lower back through injection. These cells travel all the way to the brain and help the recovery of the patient. He also shares with us the proven cases with PET scans that show the improvement of his patients. He gives us his perspective as to the reasons behind why. There is a widespread disagreement, in the medical fraternity, against the ability for Stem cell therapy to improve Autism with many doctors and neurologists suggesting that there is no conclusive proof that stem cell treatment does work on autistic patients and, in fact, that this may be very dangerous for the patients. Dr Lawrence Goldstein Director at Sanford Stem Cell Clinical Center tells us over Skype why he has reservations with this application of stem-cell treatment. Dr Goldstein also shares with us his vast understanding when it comes to stem cells in general and why he thinks this procedure might be risky. According to Dr Goldstein children with Autism generally show progress and that unless there is a proper clinical trial with Stem Cell therapy for Autism, it can never be clear that this treatment actually works. Andelene Thysse, who has an autistic son, runs a De Grendel home and learning centre for Autistic children. She believes that this procedure works and that it is the shining light that Autism patients, and their parents alike, have been waiting for. According to Andelene some of the kids she takes care of have shown immense progress in a very short space of time since they received the treatment from Dr Alok Sharma. She shares with us the improvements she has seen in the kids since they were treated. A top South African Neurologist, Dr David Griessel takes a look at some of the PET scans from Dr Alok’s patients that have shown the supposed improvement. The Neurologist will also impart his knowledge of stem cells and whether he believes the treatment can cure Autism. Furthermore, Dr Griessel will give his considered medical opinion on whether this is a viable option for autistic people. Jacinta Waruru and Mimie Ralph share with us the improvements they have observed in their Autistic children. They describe to us how their kids have been behaving differently and whether they believe in this procedure or not. Is this a procedure they would recommend to other parents? The parents also discuss the financial implications that are involved with having this procedure done. Is it an affordable route for all parents? The issue remains that Autism is a frustrating condition for parents who have Autistic kids, but when there is no ray of light for them can they really sit back and fold their arms? With Dr Sharma’s treatment clearly being supported by some parents, is this the medical discovery that the world has been waiting for or is it just another medical scam for the desperate?
